# In Defense of the Dark

Drive past the last town until the asphalt gives up and becomes gravel, then dirt. Pull over wherever the land opens wide enough to hold a horizon. Kill the engine. Turn off the headlights. And then do the hardest part: wait. Twenty minutes, half an hour. Your pupils widen; a pigment called rhodopsin rebuilds itself in your retinas, and slowly the world returns — not the world you left behind, but another one. First the bright planets. Then the ordinary stars, in numbers that seem like an accounting error. Then, if the season is right and the moon is absent, the Milky Way rises like smoke from horizon to horizon, so dense and structured it looks less like light than weather. On the finest nights, Venus is bright enough to cast your shadow on the ground. You may feel, briefly, that you are falling upward.

For almost everyone alive today, this scene requires a pilgrimage. We plan for it the way earlier generations planned for eclipses. Yet for the entire span of human history until roughly yesterday, this darkness was simply *outside*. Night was humanity's original habitat, the backdrop against which everything we are — language, religion, storytelling, music, rest itself — took shape. In the space of about two centuries, and mostly in the last eighty years, we have engineered it away. We treat this as progress, and much of it is. But it is worth pausing to ask what exactly we traded, because the receipt is longer than we tend to admit.

Start with how dark it actually was. On a moonless night before the industrial era, the countryside went black in a way that would strike a modern person as almost pathological. Long journeys were scheduled around the full moon, which served as the poor man's lantern; farmers blessed the harvest moon for letting them gather crops after sundown. Otherwise, travel stopped. Doors were bolted, fires banked, animals brought in. Many European towns rang a bell at a fixed evening hour — the *couvre-feu*, literally "cover fire" — ordering households to smother their flames and seal themselves in. Watchmen patrolled, crying the hour. The mind filled the vacuum: the "mare" of nightmare was understood to be an actual demon that climbed onto sleepers' chests. The historian Roger Ekirch, who reconstructed nightly life in the early modern West, described night as a kind of *terra incognita* — feared, respected, inhabited by rumor. And yet the dark country was not only fearful. It had its own economy and its own pleasures: spinning and mending, gossip across fences, courtship by hearth-glow, stories told precisely because there was nothing else to look at. Night, for our ancestors, was not the day switched off. It was a neighboring nation with its own customs.

It even had its own architecture of sleep. Ekirch, combing through diaries, letters, medical manuals, and court records, documented a pattern that startled him: before artificial light, people in Europe — and apparently in many other societies — slept in two segments. There was a "first sleep," begun shortly after dusk. Then people woke, naturally and calmly, for an hour or two around midnight, an interval sometimes called "the watch." They prayed. They read by rushlight. They talked. They visited neighbors. Couples made love — old medical texts even suggested this was the best time to conceive a child. People reflected on their dreams, which they remembered more readily for waking in the middle of the night. Samuel Pepys recorded getting up in the small hours to joke with his wife. Chaucer's characters retire "after the firste sleep." Anthropologists working in Nigeria recorded the same two-part rhythm. And in the 1990s the researcher Thomas Wehr essentially rebuilt the preindustrial night in a laboratory: volunteers given fourteen hours of darkness per day spontaneously began sleeping in two bouts, with a quiet, alert interlude between them. What we now file under "disorder" — waking at two in the morning, staring at the ceiling — may partly be an echo of that older rhythm, a door in the night that we boarded over. The midnight hour wasn't insomnia. It was a room of its own, and we stopped visiting it.

The conquest began modestly. A rushlight — a peeled rush dipped in kitchen fat — gave a smoky flame worth a few pennies of illumination. Tallow candles stank and guttered; wax candles cost real money; the splendid spermaceti candles of the whaling age were luxuries. For the poor, darkness was rationed: you spent light like currency. Then came gas. In 1807 the entrepreneur Frederick Winsor ran pipes along Pall Mall in London and lit the street with flames fed through the walls, to the astonishment of passersby. Within a generation, cities across Europe and America glowed; Paris, strung with tens of thousands of lanterns and then gas jets, earned the name *la Ville Lumière*, the City of Light. Then, on September 4, 1882, Thomas Edison threw the switch at Pearl Street Station in Lower Manhattan, sending electricity to fifty-nine customers — among them the offices of J.P. Morgan — and night began its final retreat. Arc lamps blazed over intersections. Factories discovered they could run in the dark hours; the night shift was born, and with it the very idea of doing anything "around the clock." Major-league baseball played its first night game in 1935, and the crowd reportedly gasped more at the lights than the plays. Night was demoted from a place to a scheduling problem. It became, in effect, off-peak daylight.

The retreat accelerated. Cheap, efficient, bluish-white LEDs flooded the world in the twenty-first century, and because they are so cheap, we use ever more of them — brighter storefronts, floodlit billboards, sports fields blazing at 2 a.m. Satellite measurements suggest the sky's artificial glow is now brightening by roughly ten percent a year. A landmark 2016 atlas calculated that more than eighty percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies, and that about a third of all people — including sixty percent of Europeans and nearly eighty percent of North Americans — can no longer see the Milky Way from home. Astronomers rank night skies on the Bortle scale, from Class 1, the pristine dark of wilderness, to Class 9, inner-city glare. Most residents of wealthy countries live out their lives between 7 and 9, under a dome of scattered light that turns night into a kind of perpetual, dirty twilight. We live beneath a lid of our own making and rarely notice, because we have never been shown the alternative.

Occasionally, the lid cracks. During the blackouts of the Second World War, when coastal cities were ordered dark against enemy bombers, Londoners reportedly saw the Milky Way arching over the rooftops for the first time in decades — an accidental planetarium produced by catastrophe. It happened again, unbidden, at 4:31 a.m. on January 17, 1994, when an earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles and people stumbled outside into the sudden blackness. Some of them called emergency services and the Griffith Observatory, alarmed, to ask about the enormous silvery cloud hanging over the city. It was the Milky Way — the galaxy we live inside — and for many callers it was a first sighting, mistaken for a phenomenon, an omen, perhaps a UFO. There is something quietly devastating in that image: an entire metropolis meeting its own galaxy as though it were an intruder.

The losses are not only aesthetic. Sea turtle hatchlings are programmed to scuttle toward the brighter horizon, which for fifty million years meant moonlight and starlight glittering on water; a beachfront glowing with resorts sends thousands of them marching inland to die, which is why coastal towns increasingly dim to amber during nesting season. Songbirds migrate at night, navigating partly by the stars; on a single October night in 2020, nearly a thousand of them died striking one illuminated building in Chicago, and studies consistently show that simply switching such lights off collapses the death toll. Even corals, which synchronize their mass spawning to the faint lunar calendar, are thrown off tempo by coastal skyglow. And insects fall victim in an unexpected way: researchers recently discovered that moths aren't really attracted to lamps so much as hijacked by them. Their instinct is to keep their backs toward the brightest thing in view — normally the sky — so a streetlight traps them in endless, exhausting circles, a snare disguised as love. Every ecosystem runs a night shift, and we are flooding its workplace.

We pay biologically, too. Scientists have identified cells in the human retina whose sole job is tracking ambient brightness; they feed the brain's master clock and govern the release of melatonin, the hormone of darkness. Blue-rich light — the spectrum of LEDs and of the screens in our hands — suppresses melatonin with particular efficiency, telling our bodies it is noon at midnight. The World Health Organization's cancer agency classifies shift work that disrupts circadian rhythms as a probable human carcinogen. Most of us are not shift workers, but we carry a portable sun in our pockets and sleep beneath the glow of charging indicators. We are the most artificially lit, worst-rested generation in history, and we puzzle over our insomnia as though the cause were hidden.

There is also an inheritance at stake that is harder to price. The night sky is the oldest library humans ever owned. Every culture wrote in it: Greeks hung their myths there; Polynesian navigators memorized star-paths that carried them across thousands of kilometers of featureless Pacific; farmers read the Pleiades for planting time. Strikingly, some of the deepest entries were composed in darkness itself. To Aboriginal Australian eyes, the dark lanes threading the Milky Way form the Emu in the Sky — a constellation made of shadow, whose position in some communities signaled when real emus were laying eggs worth gathering. Inca astronomers traced a celestial llama, a toad, a fox in those same black channels. When light pollution erases the Milky Way, it does not merely delete pretty dots; it burns a wing of the library, including the volumes written in an ink we are only learning to read. Something subtler goes with it, too: the nightly lesson in scale. A child who sees Saturn's rings through a backyard telescope, or simply stands beneath a sky thick with stars, absorbs a humility that no screen delivers. Painters knew this once — van Gogh worked by gaslight to capture the café terraces of Arles at night, and the following year, from an asylum window, painted a sky that still outshines the town beneath it. Art chased the night because the night was worth chasing.

Honesty requires the other side of the ledger. Premodern night was genuinely dangerous, and much of our ancestral fear was earned: fire, violence, and illness moved more freely in the dark. Artificial light bought real goods — reading hours for ordinary people, streets that many can walk with less fear, surgeons operating at three in the morning, the giddy beauty of a neon skyline. When Jun'ichirō Tanizaki mourned electric light in his 1933 essay *In Praise of Shadows*, he was not arguing for darkness everywhere; he was arguing for the dignity of shadow, for light that leaves something to the imagination. The problem today is not illumination. It is indiscriminateness: light without aim, without warmth, without timing, spilled upward into a sky where nobody needs it.

The remedy is refreshingly mundane, because light obeys design. It starts absurdly small: close your curtains, redirect the porch lamp so it shines down rather than into the neighbor's window and the sky beyond. Then the civic version: shield fixtures so they throw light downward, choose warm colors below 3000 kelvin, dim streets after midnight when they stand empty, trigger security lights with motion instead of letting them burn like vigil candles. Do this and you save money, spare wildlife, protect sleep — and the sky repays you with astonishing speed. Unlike carbon dioxide, light pollution washes out within hours of the switch being thrown. The stars are the most reversible casualty of civilization. Some places learned early. Flagstaff, Arizona — where Pluto was spotted in 1930 through the telescopes of Lowell Observatory — passed one of the country's first outdoor-lighting ordinances in 1958 and became the world's first certified Dark Sky City in 2001. Since the conservation group now called DarkSky International began its work in 1988, the protected map has blossomed: the island of Sark in the Channel Islands, the Central Idaho Reserve, the Aoraki Mackenzie basin in New Zealand, whole Welsh hilltops. Astro-tourism has turned preserved darkness into livelihoods, which is an argument even a budget committee can hear.

So go, at least once a year, and collect what is owed to you. Pick a moonless week, drive past the edge of the light, and grant yourself the thirty minutes your retinas request; bring a red flashlight if you must bring one, because red barely disturbs the dark. Find the band of the Milky Way, then lose yourself along its length. Know that even this is not absolute black — the upper atmosphere emits a faint green shimmer called airglow, so the natural night has a floor, a breath of luminosity, but only just. Look for Andromeda on autumn evenings, a smudge above the northeastern horizon: its light has traveled two and a half million years to reach you, older than our species by a comfortable margin. Stand inside all that. The dark is not an emptiness we improved upon. It is the oldest thing we ever lived with — the first ceiling over every campfire, the screen on which our ancestors projected everything they hoped and feared. We pushed it back so far that we forgot it was there. It is still there. Thirty miles, thirty minutes, and it returns: whole, patient, indifferent to everything except whether we bother to look up.
